layers.basics: A program stores values in variables, makes decisions with if/else, repeats with loops, and packages steps into functions.
layers.deeper: C gives close control of memory and is the language of firmware; Python is fast to write and good for analysis and test automation.
layers.expert: Static vs dynamic typing; value vs reference semantics; stack frames; arrays are contiguous memory and indexing is pointer arithmetic.

title: The C language
summary: The lingua franca of hardware-near code.

layers.basics: C maps almost directly to machine instructions; you manage memory yourself.
layers.deeper: Pointers, structs, bit operations and the preprocessor are the everyday tools of firmware developers.
layers.expert: Undefined behaviour (signed overflow, out-of-bounds, strict aliasing) is why careful style standards such as MISRA C exist.

title: Data structures
summary: Lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables.

layers.basics: A data structure organises data so common operations are fast: arrays for indexing, linked lists for insertion, trees for ordered search.
layers.deeper: Embedded code favours fixed-size ring buffers and state tables; simulators use sparse matrices.
layers.expert: Amortised analysis; balanced trees O(log n); hash tables O(1) average; ring buffer is the standard UART/DMA queue.

title: Algorithms, sorting and complexity
summary: How work grows with problem size.

layers.basics: Algorithms are recipes; complexity says how running time grows as inputs grow. Sorting is the classic example.
layers.deeper: FFT turns an O(N²) DFT into O(N log N), which is why spectrum analysers and OFDM radios are practical.
layers.expert: Big-O/Θ/Ω; comparison sort lower bound Ω(n log n); divide and conquer master theorem; P vs NP.

layers.basics: Array-based languages make it easy to simulate signals and systems and to plot results.
layers.deeper: Scripts compute filter responses, FFTs and Monte Carlo noise studies; NumPy/SciPy and MATLAB cover similar ground.
layers.expert: Vectorisation avoids interpreted loops; sparse and BLAS-backed linear algebra; toolboxes for control, signals and communications; reproducible notebooks.

layers.basics: In embedded C you write directly to hardware registers via pointers and work within a few kilobytes of memory.
layers.deeper: Memory-mapped I/O, volatile, bit masks, interrupt service routines and linker scripts define the style.
layers.expert: Stack, heap, .data, .bss, .text sections; volatile prevents optimisation of device reads; atomicity of shared variables between ISR and main loop; alignment and endianness.

ext.title: Wikipedia: Memory-mapped I/O and port-mapped I/O

layers.basics: An HDL describes digital hardware, not a sequence of steps: everything described runs in parallel.
layers.deeper: Synthesis tools turn the description into gates on an FPGA or ASIC; testbenches simulate it first.
layers.expert: RTL style: always @(posedge clk) for registers, continuous assignments for logic; blocking vs non-blocking assignments; inferred latches as classic bug; SystemVerilog assertions for verification.

layers.basics: Circuit simulators solve the circuit equations numerically so you can test a design before building it.
layers.deeper: SPICE (also LTspice, Multisim) models devices and runs DC, AC, transient and noise analyses; Simulink models block-diagram systems.
layers.expert: Modified nodal analysis assembles one matrix of KCL equations; Newton–Raphson per timestep; device models (BSIM, Gummel–Poon) are only as good as their parameters. COMSOL and HFSS solve field problems by finite elements.

layers.basics: Field solvers divide a physical structure into small elements and solve Maxwell’s or heat equations numerically.
layers.deeper: Used for antennas, PCB traces, magnetic cores and thermal design where closed forms do not exist.
layers.expert: Mesh refinement and convergence; port definitions; absorbing boundaries (PML); FDTD vs FEM vs method of moments trade-offs.
